written.text: Write a precis of the following passage.(10) The greatness of a nation is often measured by its economic prowess or military strength, yet the true bedrock of a stable society lies in the character and ethical conduct of its individual citizens. Character is not an inherited trait but a cultivated habit, forged in the crucible of daily choices and social interactions. In a world increasingly driven by material competition, the virtues of empathy, integrity, and self-discipline are frequently sidelined as antiquated ideals. However, history demonstrates that without a strong moral compass, the most sophisticated civilizations eventually crumble under the weight of internal greed and social fragmentation. Education plays a pivotal role in this character-building process, though its current trajectory often leans dangerously toward mere vocational training. True education should aim at the “refinement of the soul,” encouraging individuals to look beyond personal gain toward the collective welfare. When citizens prioritize their duties over their rights, the social fabric strengthens, creating an environment where justice and harmony can flourish naturally. This transition from “self-centeredness” to “social-consciousness” is the hallmark of a mature society. Moreover, leadership in such a society must not be defined by the exercise of power, but by the spirit of service. A leader who lacks integrity cannot inspire a nation to greatness, regardless of their intellectual brilliance. Therefore, the pursuit of ethical excellence is not merely a personal spiritual journey but a fundamental civic necessity for the survival and prosperity of any organized human community.

written.text: follow: The small hill station looked especially beautiful after the rain. Drops of water still clung to the pine needles, and a thin mist floated slowly across the valley. Binya walked carefully along the narrow mountain path with a basket of apricots balanced on her head. The earth smelled fresh and clean, and from somewhere in the forest came the soft call of a cuckoo. At the edge of the road stood an old cherry tree. Beneath it sat Grandfather Hari, wrapped in a faded woollen shawl, watching the clouds drift over the hills. Every morning, he came to the same spot with his walking stick and a small tin cup of tea. “Good morning, Grandfather,” Binya called cheerfully. “Ah, Binya,” he replied with a smile. “You are late today.” “The rain flooded the lower path,” she explained. “I had to walk through the forest trail.” Grandfather Hari nodded slowly. “The forest keeps many secrets after rain,” he said. “When I was young, I once lost my way there for two whole days.” Binya laughed. “You must have been frightened!” “Not frightened,” he said thoughtfully. “Only lonely. But the trees became my friends. In the hills, one is never truly alone.” A cool wind rustled through the branches above them. For a few moments neither spoke. They listened to the distant sound of cowbells and the steady murmur of the river far below. Then Grandfather Hari pointed toward a small green shoot growing beside the cherry tree. “That little plant was only a seed when your father was a boy,” he said proudly. “Now look at it. Someday it will give shade to travellers long after we are gone.” Binya looked at the young tree quietly. Somehow, the hills suddenly seemed older and wiser than before.
